# Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns — facts

## How it works

- [statement] Raising trigger concurrency without checking downstream capacity can exceed external API rate limits and increase database workload. MongoDB also warns that unordered execution trades guaranteed event order for parallelism; treating concurrency as a free performance improvement is unsafe. (low confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/database-triggers.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns
- [statement] Treating Trigger delivery as exactly once makes non-idempotent side effects unsafe: Atlas documents that Triggers may deliver duplicate events when failure or error conditions occur. Design repeated handling to be safe. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/databases/best-practices-and-tutorial-using-google-cloud-functions-mongodb-atlas
- [statement] Raising Trigger concurrency without checking downstream API quotas can overload external services or increase cluster load. MongoDB explicitly warns about both effects; its general guidance also recommends reducing network calls and filtering irrelevant events before invocation. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/database-triggers.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/database-triggers.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Assuming a failed Atlas Function automatically retries is an anti-pattern: the documented Function runtime has no built-in retry behavior. Custom recursive retries need a maximum attempt count and may need throttling; all recursive attempts share one invocation's execution budget. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions/handle-errors.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns
- [statement] Logging credentials is a concrete risk when adapting tutorials: Autodesk's example prints newly issued access and refresh tokens. MongoDB also documents that Function arguments are logged by default and provides a switch to disable that logging. Review both explicit log statements and automatic argument logging before passing secrets. (high confidence) Sources: https://aps.autodesk.com/blog/maintaining-refresh-tokens-mongodb-triggers ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions.md — https://aps.autodesk.com/blog/maintaining-refresh-tokens-mongodb-triggers · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions.md
- [statement] For failure visibility, OneUptime's logging example records structured error data and rethrows the exception so execution is marked failed. Its advice supports treating catch-and-log-only handlers as an observability risk; rethrowing alone does not provide automatic Atlas Function retries. (medium confidence) — https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-03-31-mongodb-atlas-trigger-logs-monitor-debug/view · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions/handle-errors.md
- [statement] Relying on application-user data rules to constrain Database or Scheduled Trigger code is an anti-pattern. These triggers execute as a system user, and MongoDB documents that system execution bypasses rules, roles, and permissions. Autodesk's trigger example also explicitly notes full system-user access. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions.md ; https://aps.autodesk.com/blog/maintaining-refresh-tokens-mongodb-triggers — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://aps.autodesk.com/blog/maintaining-refresh-tokens-mongodb-triggers
- [statement] A unique event-ID index prevents duplicate inserts, but does not by itself guarantee a notification is delivered exactly once. In Google's sample, a notification failure after insertion is followed by a retry that returns on duplicate key before notifying again. This limitation follows from the published code, not a demonstrated Atlas Trigger defect. (low confidence) — https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/databases/best-practices-and-tutorial-using-google-cloud-functions-mongodb-atlas · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Writing changes back into a watched scope can create recursive Trigger chains, including cross-trigger chains. MongoDB warns about this configuration and supports match expressions that filter the events which invoke Functions. Filter out the Function's own output changes rather than invoking on every update. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/database-triggers.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md, https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/prevent-trigger-from-infinite-loop/15854/2
- [statement] Assuming failed Atlas Functions automatically retry is an anti-pattern: Atlas Functions have no built-in retry behavior, and MongoDB documents custom retry strategies (recursive self-call in a catch block with a maximum retry count, or a Database Trigger plus a tracking collection). This is distinct from Trigger event delivery: Atlas guarantees each event is processed at least once, and Triggers may deliver duplicate events when failure or error conditions occur (for example, a server failing before durably recording its progress). Such duplicates are a failure artifact of the delivery guarantee, not a documented Function retry mechanism. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions/handle-errors.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions/handle-errors.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md
- [statement] Unbounded recursive retries can exhaust a Function execution. MongoDB recommends a retry count limit and optional throttling; retries within one invocation share its runtime budget. Recursive retry logic must therefore stop rather than keep calling indefinitely. (medium confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions/handle-errors.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions.md
- [statement] Keeping event ordering enabled for slow Functions during bursts can build a backlog because executions run sequentially. Disabling ordering permits parallel processing but loses execution-order guarantees. Treat ordering as an explicit correctness and throughput tradeoff. (high confidence) — https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/database-triggers.md · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers.md

## Facts and statements

- [statement] A scheduled Function that serially processes an entire growing collection can exceed its runtime. Autodesk explicitly warns that its all-user token-refresh example may time out at scale; MongoDB documents a 300-second Function runtime cap. Bound the work performed in each invocation. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) — https://aps.autodesk.com/blog/maintaining-refresh-tokens-mongodb-triggers · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/functions.md
- [statement] Not every same-collection update necessarily loops: MongoDB skips the update when the two versions of the document are identical, so setting already-equal values leaves the document unmodified. A Trigger that writes a changed value (such as a trigger date) back to its own collection can still fire repeatedly, and MongoDB staff suggest tagging the Trigger's own update and filtering it out in the match expression. Sources: https://dev.to/mongodb/mongodb-optimizes-updates-to-the-same-value-1f2k ; https://www.mongodb.com/community/forums/t/how-to-stop-iteration-of-trigger-when-update-document/184396/1 — https://dev.to/mongodb/mongodb-optimizes-updates-to-the-same-value-1f2k · keywords: Trigger and Function Anti-Patterns · also: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/atlas-ui/triggers/database-triggers.md
